strengths: Closes important gap between HP and MSE convergence requirements in decentralized SGD by removing strong assumptions like uniformly bounded gradients and asymptotically vanishing noise
First demonstration of linear speed-up in the number of users in the high-probability sense for DSGD—a significant theoretical achievement

Novel technical contributions with independent interest: Lemma 2 on variance reduction in HP sense, Lemma 4 on MGF of consensus gap, Lemma 5 on MGF of 'almost decreasing' processes (sharper than centralized results)
Sharp analysis with improved or matching transient times compared to MSE rates (e.g., O(max{n/(1-λ), 1/(1-λ)²}) vs O(n/(1-λ)²) for strongly convex)
Relaxes heterogeneity assumption compared to prior work—allows gradient growth with global gradient rather than fixed bounds
Comprehensive treatment covering both non-convex and strongly convex settings with detailed proofs and well-organized presentation
Experimental validation demonstrating exponential tail decay and linear speed-up consistent with theoretical predictions
weaknesses: Bounds exhibit dimension dependence of √d (non-convex) and d (strongly convex)—unavoidable with current approach but significantly limits high-dimensional applicability and creates gap vs MSE bounds without dimension dependence

Uses maxwise bounded heterogeneity (A5) rather than average heterogeneity used in MSE analysis, contradicting the stated goal of matching MSE convergence requirements; authors acknowledge but dismiss as 'for simplicity'
Complex step-size constraints with multiple simultaneous inequalities (Theorem 1) lack practical guidance; gap between fixed step-size theory and adaptive methods in practice not addressed
Limited experimental validation: only synthetic quadratic problems tested, no real datasets, primarily strongly convex experiments despite non-convex theoretical contributions
Non-convex linear speed-up requires fixed step-size while time-varying step-size loses linear speed-up, differing from centralized setting and reducing practical applicability
Requires strong convexity of individual costs (A6) for strongly convex analysis; gradient tracking extension mentioned but not covered, limiting generality
Heterogeneity requirement x¹ᵢ = x¹ⱼ for strongly convex case adds initialization constraint, even if removable at cost of additional terms

strengths: First work to establish linear speed-up in the number of users for DSGD in high-probability sense, with O(1/√(nT)) leading term
Removes restrictive uniformly bounded gradient assumption from prior work [57], replacing with more general heterogeneity bound (A5)
Novel technical results of independent interest: Lemma 2 on variance reduction in HP sense, Lemma 5 on MGF bounds for 'almost decreasing' processes
Achieves order-optimal rates for both non-convex and strongly convex costs under standard smoothness/convexity assumptions
Transient times match or improve upon corresponding MSE results, demonstrating tightness of analysis
Well-organized presentation with clear motivation, comprehensive appendix, and helpful proof sketches in main text
Experimental validation demonstrates exponential tail decay and linear speed-up on synthetic problems
weaknesses: Bounds contain √d (non-convex) and d (strongly convex) dimension factors stemming from uniform sub-Gaussianity requirements, significantly loosening rates for high-dimensional problems relative to some MSE results
For strongly convex case, requires each individual cost f_i to be μ-strongly convex (A6), which is restrictive in federated learning; relaxation via gradient tracking acknowledged as beyond scope
Heterogeneity assumption (A5) for non-convex case is stronger than average heterogeneity used in MSE analysis [11]; justification of 'keeping proofs simple' is insufficient
Strongly convex analysis requires identical model initialization x¹_i = x¹_j for all users, limiting practical applicability
Step-size conditions are complex with multiple constraints on constant C, making practical implementation difficult; sensitivity to C not discussed
Non-convex results require knowing time horizon T in advance for fixed step-size; time-varying variants lose linear speed-up
Experiments limited to synthetic quadratic problems; lacks validation on real machine learning problems and larger network scales
Comparison with [57] incomplete: [57] handles more general PL costs; practical significance of linear speed-up unclear given O((1-λ)⁴) dependence on network connectivity

strengths: First result achieving linear speed-up in number of users for DSGD in the high-probability sense, resolving a significant open gap with MSE results
Removes restrictive assumptions from prior work (e.g., [58]): replaces uniformly bounded gradient assumption with weaker bounded heterogeneity condition (A5)

Novel technical contributions of independent interest: Lemma 2 establishes variance reduction in HP sense (σ√log(d)/√n instead of σ), Lemma 4 provides MGF bound for consensus gap under strong convexity, Lemma 5 gives sharp MGF bound for 'almost decreasing' processes sharper than centralized results
Tight analysis with transient times matching or improving upon MSE-based bounds, indicating sharpness of theory
Comprehensive theoretical treatment covering both non-convex and strongly convex cases with fixed and time-varying step-sizes, including extensions to time-varying networks
Order-optimal convergence rates for both problem classes under same conditions required for MSE convergence, closing HP/MSE gap in decentralized optimization
Experimental validation of key theoretical predictions (exponential tail decay and linear speed-up in network size)
weaknesses: Logarithmic dimension dependence (log(d) factor) in convergence rates: absent from MSE results and prior HP work [58], though authors argue it is mild and potentially unavoidable for sub-Gaussian vectors per [82]

Complex step-size selection requirements with multiple interdependent conditions: α = min{C, √n/(σ√15LT)} where C itself satisfies five inequalities, making constants non-intuitive and potentially difficult to tune in practice

Known time horizon assumption: theory assumes knowledge of T in advance for fixed step-size; unknown horizon case (Appendix F) requires time-varying step-size and loses linear speed-up—this significant limitation is relegated to appendix
Restrictive noise model: handles only light-tailed (sub-Gaussian) noise, not heavy-tailed distributions; recent centralized work extends to heavy-tailed regimes with clipping
Structural constraints: requires strong convexity of each local cost for Theorem 2 and bounded heterogeneity (A5) that is stronger than average heterogeneity bounds in [11], limiting generality
Limited experimental validation: only synthetic strongly convex quadratic problems tested; non-convex case not experimentally verified; network sizes limited to n≤100 and dimension d=50

Presentation: complex step-size conditions and notation could be simplified; the crucial role of Lemma 2 in enabling linear speed-up underemphasized in main text; comparison with centralized HP rates lacks clarity
Somewhat incremental nature: primarily adapts existing centralized techniques [31, 32, 40] to decentralized setting through careful MGF balancing rather than developing fundamentally new methods
